deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a Gauss derivation. It is a draft of elementary textbook paragraphs, marked by an archival note '[Gerlings Handschrift]' (Gerling's hand). It sits between Gauss's computations on the regular 17-gon (cos(2pi/17) periods) on the neighbouring pages, but has no connection to them.

(1) Right column, main text. Let b be a positive integer with a^n < b < (a+1)^n for some integer a.
- The n-th root of b cannot be an integer, since it would have to lie strictly between the consecutive integers a and a+1.
- It cannot be a proper fraction either. This is the cited §173. Filled in by me with the standard argument: if p/q is in lowest terms with q > 1, then p^n/q^n is also in lowest terms, so it is not an integer.
- Hence such roots (and 'incomplete powers') are called irrational: magnitudes not exactly representable by whole or fractional numbers.
- One must be content to give bounds between which they fall, by fractions and especially by decimal fractions (the cited §§142, 145, about decimal fractions).

(2) Middle column. In the successive decimal development of a root of a whole number, things go much as in §177 (presumably the digit-by-digit square-root algorithm or decimal division).
- (I) Each following part, from the first on, has a smaller order of magnitude (fewer or lower-place digits) than the one before it.
- One can carry the root as far as desired, each new part being found from the remainder of the preceding step.
- Much of this column is illegible; I give only its gist.

(3) Upside-down line: '17x = 24 + x', a trivial linear equation with solution x = 3/2. Its context is unclear.

(4) Left column, sideways and largely illegible. It refers to decimal fractions, digits, §166, and some small numerical examples ('2.1 = 2.2.9', '33', '3'). These cannot be reconstructed reliably.
errors: No mathematical errors are detectable in the legible portions.
The left sideways column and parts of the middle column are too illegible to check.

results.what: If a^n < b < (a+1)^n with a, b integers, then b^(1/n) is irrational: it is neither an integer nor a fraction.
results.modern_name: Irrationality of n-th roots of non-perfect-powers (rational root theorem special case)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euclid Book X for square roots; general case standard in textbooks)

results.what: Irrational roots are approximated by bounding fractions or decimal fractions, developed digit by digit.
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient/medieval algorithm; standard in school texts

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary textbook material on irrational roots and decimal approximation, apparently in Gerling's hand rather than Gauss's. Nothing on it is non-standard.

checkable.asserts: The upside-down equation 17x = 24 + x has solution x = 3/2.
Example of the theorem: 5 lies between consecutive squares, so sqrt(5) is irrational.
Example for n = 3: 10 lies between 8 and 27, so the cube root of 10 is irrational.
The §173 lemma in an instance: a power of a reduced fraction is still reduced, hence not an integer.

transcription_corrections: Right column, first sentence: the sense is 'Ist eine ganze Zahl b zwischen zwei auf einander folgenden n-ten Potenzen ganzer Zahlen a^n und (a+1)^n enthalten, so kann die Wurzel b^(1/n) keine ganze Zahl seyn, weil es dann eine ganze Zahl zwischen a und a+1 geben müßte'. The transcribed 'noch gäbe' is incomplete.
Middle column, opening: 'falschen' is doubtful. The context suggests 'successiven'/'solchen' Decimalbruch-Entwickelung, i.e. the successive decimal expansion of a root.
The page is in Gerling's hand per the archival note; 'Ewardy' is likely a misreading of a later archival or name annotation.
Bottom of right column: the reference reads '(§§ 142.145)' and concerns decimal fractions.
